question: How does the reference architecture enter the root hsdd-spec run: which files, with what authority?

options.label: Spec only
options.consequence: The root decomposes from the normative rules alone. Guide Appendix B (package layers) and Appendix C (what v1 ships) would be invisible, so v1 scope and the package split would rest on judgement.

options.label: Spec, Guide and Rationale, each with its authority
options.consequence: The root's Sources lists the Spec as the accepted normative source and the Guide and Rationale as informative. Downstream planners can read the Guide's Dart mappings and v1 tooling table; nothing informative can override a Spec rule.

options.label: All arch versions plus loop/
options.consequence: Superseded history would compete with v0.15.0 and the blindness rule forbids it.

chosen: Spec, Guide and Rationale, each with its authority
why: The owner's facts make the Spec accepted and frozen and the other two informative; hsdd-spec's Sources rule wants each input listed with its authority, and the Guide is the only place that says what v1 ships on Dart (Appendix C.2) and how the packages layer (Appendix B).

question: How is the run-stop condition 'two leading options change the tree's shape, the Specification is silent, no experiment settles it' read, given that the same policy lists v1 scope and decomposition shape under decide-and-record?

options.label: Literal
options.consequence: Every decomposition choice changes the tree's shape and the Spec says nothing about HSDD nodes, so the run would stop at the root on its first real choice; decide-and-record for decomposition shape would never apply.

options.label: Both defensible, no stated reason
options.consequence: The condition holds when the two leading options are both defensible, produce different nodes or contracts, and neither the Spec, the owner's facts, an experiment, nor a stated rule in the Guide, Rationale or HSDD gives one a reason to lead. Shape decisions with a stated reason are taken and recorded; the reason is cited as evidence.

why: Only this reading lets both halves of the policy apply. It keeps the stop for the case the policy is written for, a toss-up on shape that only the owner can break, and it is written into every subagent's prompt so the reading is visible and the same at every step. The signal that would have changed my mind: an owner statement that informative documents never break a shape tie.

question: The owner bans the em-dash and the phrase 'load-bearing' in prose; HSDD templates use an em-dash as a token (empty table cells, the OQ detail heading, the Collides-with reason). Which wins in HSDD artifacts?

options.label: Keep the HSDD template tokens
options.consequence: Artifacts match the templates character for character, and carry the character the owner bans.

options.label: Owner's ban, with parser-equivalent tokens
options.consequence: Empty cells and lists read `none`, OQ detail headings read `### {ID}: {title}`, a Collides-with reason is its own sentence. HSDD's parsers accept all three, so no tooling breaks.

why: The owner's prose rules are standing instructions and HSDD's own tooling treats `none` as empty and a colon as the title separator, so honoring the ban costs nothing. Formatting only: no node, contract or interface changes.

question: The inputs include 'HSDD's own documentation under ~/git/hsdd/docs/'. Does that cover docs/superpowers/ and the Claude memory directory?

options.label: Everything under ~/git/hsdd/docs/
options.consequence: Subagents could read HSDD's development plans, which discuss field tests; one of them could describe the manual run of this planning.

options.label: users-guide and the methodology spec only; no memory, no docs/superpowers/
options.consequence: Subagents keep everything the methodology needs and lose HSDD's internal development notes, which no skill requires.

chosen: users-guide and the methodology spec only; no memory, no docs/superpowers/
why: The blindness rule forbids any document describing the manual run and forbids searching for one. HSDD's development notes and the session memory are the two places in reach that plausibly describe it, and the planning needs neither.

question: In what order do decomposition and contract authoring run?

options.label: Per level
options.consequence: Root spec, its ADRs, its contracts, then recurse; each mid-level decomposition reads concrete contract bodies for the edges it inherits. A root contract may need an amendment once its producer is decomposed.

options.label: Decompose everything first
options.consequence: All hsdd-spec runs first, then every contract once the whole tree is known; fewer amendments, but mid-level splits are cut against contract names and Spec prose rather than contract bodies.

why: HSDD's greenfield workflow is hsdd-spec (root), hsdd-contract, recurse; it keeps every decomposition cut against an interface that already exists. The cost, a draft contract amended after its producer splits, is cheap while contracts are draft. The signal that would have changed my mind: a root contract that the first mid-level decomposition has to split in two.

question: When does hsdd-reconcile run: once after every leaf-parent is planned, or after each phase plan?

options.label: Once at the end
options.consequence: Mirrors the parallel-worktree model; every plan is written against the same frozen snapshot, so a producer's amend and a consumer's assumption written blind to it can collide, which this run must stop on.

options.label: After each phase plan
options.consequence: Serial flow as hsdd-reconcile lists it ('a phase plan just finished in a serial flow'); each later plan reads contracts with earlier requests answered and amends folded in, so cross-node collisions cannot form from ignorance. Costs one reconcile step per leaf-parent plus a final sweep.

why: The run is serial by rule, and with planning serial there is no reason to hide one node's settled contract from the next planner. Collisions that would come only from planning blind to an already-settled answer are artifacts of the parallel model, not design disagreements. A genuine disagreement still surfaces at the reconcile right after the plan that raises it. The signal that would have changed my mind: the owner wanting this run to exercise the parallel model's collision handling.

question: In what order are leaf-parents phase-planned?

options.label: Producer first (topological by contract edge)
options.consequence: A producer's plan, its amends and phase ids land before any consumer plans against the contract.

options.label: Tree order
options.consequence: Simpler to follow, but a consumer may plan against a contract whose producer has not settled its semantics yet.

why: With reconcile after each plan, producer-first order means each consumer reads the producer's settled contract. Ties break in tree order.

question: Which HSDD skills does this run use?

options.label: Planning skills only: hsdd-spec, hsdd-adr, hsdd-contract, hsdd-phase-plan, hsdd-reconcile
options.consequence: The run ends at reconcile as instructed; no phase context, milestone document, checkpoint or reading aid is produced.

options.label: Planning skills plus hsdd-milestone and hsdd-summary
options.consequence: The owner would also get a stakeholder milestone document and an HTML plan page, at the cost of steps outside 'through reconcile'.

chosen: Planning skills only: hsdd-spec, hsdd-adr, hsdd-contract, hsdd-phase-plan, hsdd-reconcile
why: The instruction is planning from scratch through reconcile, and the finish condition names no milestone or summary. hsdd-config is execution, hsdd-checkpoint and hsdd-intake need a running project, hsdd-adopt is brownfield.

question: Who runs experiments, and where do they land in the commit history?

options.label: The step subagent, inside its step
options.consequence: The experiment sits next to the decision it settles and lands in that step's artifact commit; the subagent spends part of its context on it.

options.label: Separate experiment subagents dispatched by the orchestrator
options.consequence: Cleaner step contexts, but every experiment breaks a step in two and the evidence lands in a commit apart from the decision.

chosen: The step subagent, inside its step
why: The decision and its evidence belong in one commit, and the subagent knows exactly which fact it needs. The orchestrator dispatches its own experiment subagent only when it needs a fact to answer a stop; that experiment is committed on its own as `experiment: <name>` and cited from the stop decision.

question: How are the skill's gates checked after each step?

options.label: Read-through only
options.consequence: The orchestrator reads every artifact against the skill's checklist; cheap to set up, and misses a stale registry or an unresolved id as easily as a person does.

options.label: Mechanical gate plus read-through
options.consequence: A dependency-free script checks write sets, the verbatim generator and a clean regeneration, id resolution, child files, Validation paths and the owner's prose bans; the orchestrator reads the rest against the subagent's self-check.

why: The protocol's three named checks (clean regeneration, frozen governance changed only by its owner, every cited id resolves) are mechanical and run after every step; a script does them the same way every time. Judgement checks stay with the read-through.
